title.en: Compound nouns: the last word sets the gender

summary.en: Long German nouns snap smaller words together, and the final building block rules the whole word.

body.en:
From season 1, episodes 1, 2 and 5.

Around the guesthouse you hear vivid joined words like *Messingschlüssel* (brass key), *Reifenpanne* (flat tyre), *Kühlschrank* (fridge), and *Zitronenkuchen* (lemon cake). Instead of stringing separate nouns together with spaces, German fuses them into one crisp compound.

Read any German compound from right to left to find its core meaning and its grammatical gender: the final noun is always the boss. Even though *die Zitrone* (lemon) is feminine, *der Kuchen* (cake) is masculine, so *der Zitronenkuchen* is masculine too.

Likewise, *der Schlüssel* gives its gender to *der Messingschlüssel*, *der Schrank* makes *der Kühlschrank* masculine, and *das Wasser* makes *das Duschwasser* neuter. Many compounds insert a smooth linking `-n-` or `-s-` between parts, while main spoken stress stays near the front.

On replay, listen for the strong stress on the first part of *Messingschlüssel*, *Kühlschrank*, and *Zitronenkuchen*.
